questions.question: Profit rose from ₹3.16 crore in FY24 to ₹11.86 crore in FY26, but only 65.5% of operating profit came in as cash. What does that suggest?

choices.text: The business is doing brilliantly; cash doesn't matter.
Some profit may be stuck in unpaid bills or unsold goods, so check how fast customers pay.
The company must have paid a big dividend.
Profit and cash are always equal, so the figures must be wrong.

questions.explanation: Profit is counted when a sale is made; cash arrives when the customer pays. For Maxwell Engineering Solutions Limited, only 65.5% of operating profit turned into cash, so money is getting stuck. Trade receivables and inventory are where to look.

questions.question: At the top price, Maxwell Engineering Solutions Limited's P/E is 13.4x. Similar listed companies have a P/E of about 92.4x. What does that tell you?

choices.text: It costs about the same as, or less than, similar companies for each rupee of profit.
It costs more than similar companies for each rupee of profit, so its profit must grow faster to be worth it.
The P/E shows how many shares the company has.

questions.explanation: A P/E of 13.4x against 92.4x means you pay no more for each rupee of Maxwell Engineering Solutions Limited's profit than for its peers'. That is a fair starting point, not a guarantee.

questions.question: Maxwell Engineering Solutions Limited owes 0.67 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0.67 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, Maxwell Engineering Solutions Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.
